title: Yarn Properties and Applications of Ring-Spun, Rotor-Spun, Core-Spun and Filament Yarns
description: Read article about This article compares ring-spun, rotor-spun, core-spun, and filament yarns by formation, structure, properties, applications, and selection criteria for textile use. and more articles about Textile industry at Fibre2Fashion
head:
Key Takeaways
Ring-spun yarns offer strength, fineness, and softness, while rotor-spun yarns prioritise productivity, evenness, low hairiness, and cost efficiency in medium and coarse counts.
Core-spun yarns use a filament core and staple-fibre sheath for stretch, stability, or strength, while filament yarns provide continuous, engineered structures for apparel and technical uses.
markdown:
Yarn provides the structural link between fibre and fabric, and its performance is governed by both fibre characteristics and spinning or yarn-forming technology. The same fibre can produce yarns with substantially different strength, evenness, hairiness, handle and end-use performance when processed through different systems. This article examines ring-spun, rotor-spun, core-spun and filament yarns (Figure 1) in terms of their formation, structure–property relationships and principal applications.

Figure 1: Longitudinal and cross-sectional view of (a) ring-spun, (b) rotor-spun, (c) core-spun, (d) flat filament and (e) textured filament yarns.

Ring-Spun Yarn

Ring spinning is a mature and widely used staple-fibre spinning system. Roving is drafted to the required fineness between pairs of rollers (Figure 2). The drafted strand then passes through a traveller running around a ring. Differential spindle and traveller speeds insert twist while simultaneously winding the yarn onto the bobbin (Lawrence, 2010).

Figure 2: Ring spinning process

Structure and Properties

Ring-spun yarn consists of fibres arranged predominantly in helical paths around the yarn axis (Figure 1a), with fibre migration between the core and surface. This structure provides effective fibre cohesion and contributes to high strength, flexibility and a soft handle. Ring spinning also accommodates a wide range of yarn counts, from fine to coarse. Its principal limitation is surface hairiness, caused by fibre ends protruding from the twisted structure; excessive hairiness can contribute to pilling, fly and surface irregularity.

Compact spinning modifies the ring-spinning process by condensing the fibre strand before twist insertion. The resulting structure reduces hairiness and can improve strength and evenness. However, ring spinning has lower productivity than systems such as rotor spinning because spindle and traveller speeds constrain output, while the roving and subsequent winding stages add processing requirements and cost.

Applications

Ring-spun yarns are selected for products requiring a combination of strength, fineness and softness. Applications include fine shirting and suiting, bed linen, premium knitwear and hosiery, sewing threads and high-quality denim. Combed and compact ring-spun yarns are particularly suited to fine and premium fabrics.

Rotor-Spun Yarn

Rotor spinning, or open-end spinning, feeds sliver directly into the spinning unit and therefore eliminates the roving stage. An opening roller separates the sliver into individual fibres, which are transported by an air stream into a rapidly rotating rotor (Figure 3). The fibres collect in the rotor groove, where rotation forms them into yarn. The yarn is then withdrawn and wound directly into a cross-wound package. Elimination of roving and separate winding operations is a major economic advantage of the system (Lawrence, 2010).

Figure 3: Rotor (open-end) spinning process

Structure and Properties

Rotor-spun yarn has a twisted fibre core surrounded by wrapper fibres, often described as belts (Figure 1b). Compared with ring-spun yarn of similar count, rotor yarn generally has lower strength because fibre alignment and straightness are lower and wrapper fibres contribute less effectively to tensile performance. Its structure supports good evenness, relatively low hairiness and reduced tendency to pill. The yarn is generally firmer in handle because rotor spinning commonly requires higher twist, and the system is most suitable for medium and coarse counts.

Rotor spinning can also process shorter fibres, including comber noil and recycled cotton. This expands its relevance to economical yarn production and recycled-fibre applications.

Applications

Rotor-spun yarn is appropriate where productivity, evenness and cost efficiency are important and maximum strength or softness is not the primary requirement. Common applications include denim, towels, heavy knitted fleece, workwear, bed sheeting, home furnishings and industrial fabrics.

Core-Spun Yarn

Core-spun yarn combines a continuous filament core with a staple-fibre sheath. In a typical modified ring-spinning process, the filament is introduced at the front roller while drafted staple fibres are twisted around it (Figure 4). Core-spun yarns can also be produced using rotor, air-jet and friction systems. The core may be a rigid filament such as polyester or an elastic component such as elastane; bicomponent filaments such as PET/PTT (T400) may also be used.

Figure 4: Core-spun yarn production on a modified ring-spinning system.

Structure and Properties

The core–sheath structure (Figure 1c) integrates different functions within one yarn. The core contributes strength, dimensional stability or stretch, while the sheath determines surface handle, appearance, comfort and dyeability. A cotton sheath, for example, can provide a cotton-like surface while the filament core contributes functional performance.

Process control is critical to core-spun yarn quality. For elastane-core yarns, the draft applied to the elastane before insertion affects yarn count accuracy, twist, elongation and imperfections and can influence the tensile and tear performance of the resulting fabric. Core exposure (grin-through) and sheath slippage are important defects requiring control (Hossain et al., 2024).

Recent development has extended the structure to dual-core and tri-core yarns, in which elastic and rigid or semi-elastic components are combined to balance stretch, recovery and strength. Research on tri-core yarns containing cotton sheaths with T400 and elastane cores has shown that the arrangement of core components affects both yarn and fabric performance (Babaarslan et al., 2025).

Applications

Core-spun yarns are used where a functional filament core is required without losing the surface characteristics of a staple fibre. Major applications include polyester-core sewing threads, elastane-core stretch denim and woven fabrics, burn-out (devoré) fabrics, and protective or technical textiles.

Filament Yarn

Filament yarns are formed from one or more continuous filaments rather than staple fibres and therefore do not require conventional staple-fibre spinning. Monofilament yarn contains a single filament, whereas multifilament yarn contains multiple fine filaments grouped together, usually with little or no twist. Most filament yarns are manufactured from polymers such as polyester, nylon, polypropylene and viscose; silk is the principal natural filament. Flat filament yarns are smooth and compact (Figure 1d), while texturing processes such as false-twist and air-jet texturing introduce crimp, loops or bulk (Figure 1e) to modify stretch, cover and handle (McIntyre, 2005).

Production of Nylon Filament Yarn

Nylon filament yarn is produced by melt spinning. Nylon 6,6 is synthesised by condensation polymerisation of hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid, whereas nylon 6 is produced by ring-opening polymerisation of caprolactam. Residual caprolactam in nylon 6 is removed by hot-water extraction. Polymer chips are dried to a controlled moisture content before melting because moisture influences melt viscosity; in continuous plants, polymer melt may instead be fed directly to the spinning machine.

The chips are melted in a screw extruder at a temperature above the polymer melting point, which is approximately 220 °C for nylon 6 and 260 °C for nylon 6,6. A metering pump delivers the melt at a constant rate through the filter media of the spin pack to the spinneret. The extruded filaments are solidified by cross-flow air in a quench chamber, and a spin finish is applied (Figure 5). In fully drawn yarn (FDY) production, the filaments pass from a feed godet to a heated draw godet running at a higher surface speed; the ratio of the two speeds is the draw ratio. Drawing aligns the polymer chains and develops crystallinity, which increases tenacity and reduces elongation, while the heated godet also heat-sets the yarn. An interlacing air jet entangles the filaments to provide cohesion in place of twist before winding. Partially oriented yarn (POY) is instead wound at high speed without full drawing and is subsequently drawn and textured by the false-twist process. High-tenacity nylon yarns for tyre cord and industrial fabrics are produced from higher-molecular-weight polymer at higher draw ratios (McIntyre, 2005).

Figure 5: Nylon filament melt-spinning and drawing process

Structure and Properties

The continuous structure provides high uniformity and can support high strength because there are no staple-fibre ends and limited inter-fibre slippage. Flat filament yarns have a smooth, lustrous surface and essentially no staple-fibre hairiness. They generally exhibit low pilling but may be susceptible to snagging depending on fabric construction. Synthetic flat filaments also tend to have low moisture absorption and may feel smooth, cool or slippery; texturing increases bulk and improves handle. Filament fineness, cross-section, lustre and filament number can be engineered during fibre production, enabling controlled performance characteristics.

Applications

Flat filament yarns are used in linings, lingerie, sarees, dress fabrics, curtains and umbrella fabrics. Textured filament yarns are used in hosiery, sportswear, activewear and knitted fabrics. High-tenacity filament yarns serve technical applications including tyre cord, seat belts, ropes and industrial fabrics.

Selection of Yarn Type

Yarn selection is a product-specific decision based on the required balance of mechanical performance, handle, appearance, processing efficiency and cost. Ring-spun yarn is appropriate where fine counts, strength and softness are required. Rotor-spun yarn is suited to economical production of relatively even, low-hairiness yarns in medium and coarse counts. Core-spun yarn is selected when the surface characteristics of a staple fibre must be combined with the strength, stability or stretch of a filament. Filament yarn is appropriate when continuous structure, smoothness, lustre, high strength or engineered performance is required.

Table 1: Comparative characteristics and applications of ring-spun, rotor-spun, core-spun and filament yarns.

| Feature | Ring-spun | Rotor-spun | Core-spun | Filament |
| Fibre form | Staple | Staple | Filament core + staple sheath | Continuous filament |
| Formation | Spindle/traveller twist | Rotor-based twist | Staple fibres around core | Filament extrusion |
| Structure | Predominantly helical fibres | Twisted core + wrapper fibres | Core–sheath | Continuous filaments |
| Relative strength | High | Generally lower than ring | Depends on core and sheath | Generally high |
| Hairiness | Relatively higher | Relatively low | Depends on sheath | Very low in flat filament |
| Handle | Soft | Firmer | Engineered through sheath/core | Smooth; modified by texturing |
| Typical counts | Fine to coarse | Medium to coarse | Wide range | Engineered fineness |
| Major applications | Apparel, hosiery, premium fabrics | Denim, towels, home textiles | Stretch and functional fabrics | Apparel and technical textiles |
